title: Uncle Tomming, Dizzy Gillespie's quote and selling to whites
summary: Prompted by a Gillespie quote, Tex discusses accommodating whites, his own experience selling advertising, and everyone selling.

people.name: To Be or Not to Bop (book)

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: This is the thing from, this is from Dizzy Gillespie's, we talked about Uncle Tommy and Dizzy has something from his autobiography to be or not to Bob and Dizzy's your age, so him making this, he says, he says, I had my own way of Tommy. Every generation of blacks in slavery has had to develop its own way of Tommy, of accommodating itself to a basically unjust situation. Do you agree with what he said?
And can you, how does it manifest itself?

Well, it manifests itself in a very simple way. You're dealing with a financial kind of situation where you have to survive to get along with white folks and other words you had to develop a certain type of vocalization or a certain manner of reason when dealing with white folks. When you start talking about a job, when you start talking about social activities or anything, you sort of play the low road instead of elevate yourself to the high road, regardless of, because after all, sometimes you just had to do it. But today, most young blacks would not do that because they feel or believe that they got it made. But we are in worse trouble as blacks today because we have, well, you see, major corporations today are downsizing.

And it's affecting you, it's affecting the economy right now. But I can remember many a days when even myself, I had to take the low road in dealing with whites. Even today, in selling advertising, when I call on corporate people to sell advertising, I have to mellow myself a little bit, but I do my feasibility study and my homework because I know before I call on this individual, I just about know what he's like, who he is, and where he's coming from and what he likes, what his social background. Otherwise, I do a study before I call on any major corporation to find out how far I can go with him. And of course, now like I said, I take a different posture today. I can sit back and say, look, I'm a college trained person, I'm a businessman, I came to do business with you, but I'm not going to kiss you behind. You know, one of these kind of things, you know. And then again, here's the best way, I wouldn't say, I wouldn't call it Toman, but I could say, well, here you are with one of the finest organizations, financially and socially, in the greater metropolitan area of New Orleans. You are well established. You work with the community chess. You work with the port of embarkation. You're doing a lot of things to help the growth of the city of New Orleans with this image. We're proud to represent you. You know, these kind of things I would tell him or whoever is there, make him feel good about him or herself. I wouldn't say, well, I guess that's a way of Toman, but it's a way of selling too because anything you do, you're selling. You know, like a guy told me one day, well, I can't sell. I said, yes, you can. You're a master craft. I never sold nothing in my life. I say, you sell every day and every night. What do you mean I'm selling every day? Do you get on your knees and say, our father? That's selling, brother. And no, I bet that's the greatest sales job you ever do the long you live. It's the greatest sales job you ever do. So getting on your knees saying, our father. Okay.
